name: Bilal Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What fills a normal day on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and lead the carpenters building timber forms around concrete columns on building sites. I have a trade certificate and enough hard jobs behind me that the crew trusts my measurements. My pay is above the usual rate, and my partner and I have grown children and more than six months of expenses saved. I have never used an AI tool; I want to finish regular site work at sixty-five in 2033 if our income actually covers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office can count timber faster, but we still build the form and check its braces. An AI formwork list will not stop wet concrete pushing a weak column form apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my good wage and lead role to continue. We have over six months saved and plenty of builders nearby, so a small ordering change is not a threat to the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep measuring column forms and checking braces before the pour. I would ask my partner to put expected age-sixty-five income beside our household bills before calling retirement affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the work. I do not need a computer to see whether a brace is properly fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check before a column pour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every brace, tie and base fixing against the site specification. I walk around the form with another carpenter before the concrete truck is called.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why review retirement figures if work looks safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a date on the calendar does not pay the bills. The check is information; I would keep earning until the figures work.

say: I would **keep** testing braces and ties before a concrete pour.
I would **let** the office speed its timber count without changing my site checks.
think: **High** pay, strong savings and many nearby builders keep this secure.
The **age-sixty-five** target still needs verified household income.
do: **Keep** leading column formwork and checking braces before pours.
**Review** expected age-sixty-five household income against housing, food and repair bills with my partner.
S0.quote: An AI formwork list will not stop wet concrete pushing a weak column form apart.
fieldNote: **Bilal** has never used AI and leads physical formwork safety checks with a trade certificate.
**Higher** pay, over six months saved and many nearby jobs make a small office improvement manageable.

steps.text: Keep leading and inspecting building-site column forms
Check age-sixty-five retirement budget before deciding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say faster buying is welcome if the timber arrives before the form crew needs it. A faster AI concrete schedule could leave my formwork crew checking braces off the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my basic site role is likely safe for now, though a builder could trim overtime between pours. We could manage that with savings, but I would still want the rate and hours written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the column work and compare paid checking hours across two pours. If those hours shrink, I would ask the builder for written terms and look at posted local formwork jobs only where wages cover our household and safety time is paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut to my own hours, not frightened of the program itself. I would use a measured record rather than learn an AI screen I do not need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which hours would you record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The time from final brace check to the concrete arriving, and whether the crew was paid for it. Two pours would show if a new schedule changed that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a new job immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only a posted nearby role with a clear household-covering wage and paid safety checks. Plenty of builders exist, but I would not resign on a rumour.

say: I would **compare** actual paid brace-check time across two pours.
I would **ask** the builder for written wage and safety-hour terms if time shrinks.
think: My **overtime** could fall even if the main formwork job remains.
**Savings** provide room to choose a real local alternative.
do: **Keep** paid column shifts while recording brace-check hours on two pours.
**Look** after paid-hour cuts at posted local formwork jobs with household-covering wages and paid safety checks.
feel: **Anxious** about possible own-hour loss, with strong alternatives.
S1.quote: A faster AI concrete schedule could leave my formwork crew checking braces off the clock.
fieldNote: He **remains** pragmatic: record actual paid safety time and compare written local offers.
A **plausible** overtime cut affects his own income despite strong savings; he does not invent a need to learn AI.

steps.text: Keep paid formwork while logging brace-check hours
Look after cuts at posted local formwork jobs with household-covering wages and paid safety checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI can plan a column in 2028 when I am sixty, but hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. That is two years before the age-sixty-five retirement I hope for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot-built column in 2031 could take my pay before it takes responsibility for a safe pour. Strong savings and many local builders give me options, but neither proves that our income can support leaving two years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid crew and ask the builder for a supervised paid place checking robot-built braces, with authority to stop a pour; a request is not a trial already run. If my hours are cut, I would apply only to posted local repair-formwork roles with household-covering pay and written safe access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible two-year gap, but I can search and check the retirement figures. I would not stop at sixty-three without verified income for the years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see in a robot-built form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ties and braces before concrete hides them, plus a written right to halt the pour. I would not approve from a photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend robot software training to keep the role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would rather inspect the physical form I know. If a formal course were required, it would need full funding, paid days and a posted local job paying our bills before I enrolled.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches plans in 2028; physical robots may build forms around 2031.
I would **request** an offered paid place checking braces with stop-pour authority.
think: **Two** wage years could be lost before my target, but savings are not a retirement calculation.
A **local** repair job needs an actual posting, adequate pay and safe access.
do: **Request** supervised paid robot-form checking place with stop-pour authority.
**Keep** paid column shifts unless an offered trial place exists.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local repair-formwork job with adequate pay and safe access.
feel: **Anxious** about possible final two-year wage gap, with choices.
S2.quote: A robot-built column in 2031 could take my pay before it takes responsibility for a safe pour.
fieldNote: He **requests** a paid supervised place without claiming to have run a trial.
**Formal** course interest remains conditional and untagged; his fallback requires an actual adequate safe local vacancy.

steps.text: Keep paid column shifts while requesting supervised paid checking place with stop-pour authority
Apply after cuts to posted local repair-formwork job with adequate pay and safe access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and capable site robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If my original age-sixty-five retirement in 2033 is affordable, the physical machines arrive after I leave regular site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still need the income figures. If the budget fails, I may be on a site at sixty-six and need a paid formwork or repair role with real stop-pour authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading paid column work and check our age-sixty-five income with my partner. If it covers ongoing bills, I would retire at the original target; if not, I would apply only to posted local formwork repair roles with wages that cover the household and written safe access and stop-pour authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the figures are settled. A 2034 formwork robot is my problem only if the 2033 retirement budget sends me back to site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training if a repair role required it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a posted nearby vacancy at adequate pay, with a fully funded course and paid study days. Asking the employer about it would not mean I had enrolled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the income figures have to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, food, repairs and enough margin to avoid spending the cash reserve at once. I will not leave a good wage without that calculation.

say: The 2034 **robot** date follows my planned 2033 retirement if affordable.
I would **continue** paid formwork only if the household budget falls short.
think: A **real** nearby repair role must pay bills and permit a safe stop-pour decision.
A **course** enquiry is not training without a funded paid place and posted job.
do: **Check** age-sixty-five household income against ongoing costs.
**Retire** at original 2033 target only if verified income covers bills.
**Apply** if retirement income falls short to posted local repairs with household-covering wages, safe access and stop-pour authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until budget and job conditions are verified.
S3.quote: A 2034 formwork robot is my problem only if the 2033 retirement budget sends me back to site.
fieldNote: His **pre-existing** retirement target falls before the physical robot date, and continued work is conditional.
He does **not** tag a course enquiry as retraining; any local application needs adequate pay and written safety authority.

steps.text: Check original age-sixty-five retirement budget before deciding
Retire at original 2033 target only if income covers bills
Apply if income short to posted bill-covering local repair job with safe access and stop-pour authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight and capable formwork robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A formwork robot in 2039 cannot replace a wage my household stopped needing in 2033, if our sums hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not claim I am still building columns at seventy-one. If our retirement income falls short, I could still need a nearby paid repair job for a while, but I will not count on an unposted opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the present paid column shifts and verify the age-sixty-five budget with my partner. If it covers our bills, I would retire at the original 2033 target; otherwise I would apply to posted local formwork repair work only at household-covering pay with safe access and stop-pour authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until we check the figures and calm about the distant robot date if we can leave. I would rather hand over the formwork notebook than guess about a job at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would get the formwork notebook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A younger carpenter on the crew, if the builder agrees. It lists the awkward column fixes and the checks before each pour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you still need wages after sixty-five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning only in an actual local posted role that pays our bills and lets me inspect safely. I would not rely on a robot forecast as an offer.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots may follow my original exit.
I would **keep** earning only if verified household income is short.
think: **Any** later formwork role needs a real local posting, adequate pay and safety authority.
do: **Keep** paid column work while verifying age-sixty-five retirement income.
**Retire** at original 2033 target only if income covers ongoing bills.
**Apply** if retirement income falls short to posted local repairs with household-covering wages, safe access and stop-pour authority.
feel: **Uneasy** until the household budget is checked, calmer about distant robots.
S4.quote: A formwork robot in 2039 cannot replace a wage my household stopped needing in 2033, if our sums hold.
fieldNote: His **age-sixty-five** exit is pre-existing and income-conditional, not a forced retirement.
**Later** work depends on a budget shortfall and an actual posted safe local role at household-covering pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because column robots could cut two paid years before my planned exit. A paid supervised checking place and a posted local repair job with adequate pay and stop-pour authority would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can halt a concrete pour when a robot has hidden a bad brace. I have no interest in the screen, but I will check a physical form if someone pays me to do it safely. A column form is ready when the braces hold, not when a computer says the count is right.

headlineQuote: A column form is ready when the braces hold, not when a computer says the count is right.
portrait: **Bilal** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified lead carpenter who builds column formwork.
His **higher** pay, savings beyond six months, partner, grown children and many nearby jobs give him options.
He **has** never used AI and prefers physical measurements and written safety terms.
He **hopes** to retire at sixty-five in 2033 if income covers bills; later employment is conditional.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could reduce paid formwork two years before his original age-sixty-five retirement target.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered** paid supervised checking place and a posted safe local repair job at adequate wages would help.
